## Summary

Research confidence is **Moderate**. Some of this break's ideal conditions are confirmed by sources; others rest on limited evidence. It is the class the app computes from the evidence (how well the break's ideal conditions are documented), not a forecast and not a probability.

Main gaps:

- Limited information is available about the wave sizes this break works in.
- No source on how the wave breaks has a publication date, and sandbars move, so the descriptions may be out of date.
- Limited information is available about the swell period this break needs.
- No survey, scientific or official source confirms the best swell direction.

Research notes (research_evidence.json):

> Re-read 8 of 11 sources directly; surfertoday.com, surfer.com and sciencedirect.com returned 403 and are kept unchanged as web_search. New readable sources: Journal of Coastal Research abstract (BioOne, 2012) and an Unofficial Networks surf check (2011, east wind offshore and ideal; NW-SW swells). Wind is now supported by two readable sources (surf-forecast.com and Unofficial Networks), both east = 90 deg, matching the profile. Direction: surf-forecast says west (270) and Unofficial Networks NW-SW (225-315), both consistent with the 255-295 optimum. The Inertia only says 'north swells' colloquially, so no number was recorded; it also says some mid-summer south swells miss the beach, which questions the 190 deg end of the swell window. Tide: no readable source supports the profile's 'mid'. surf-forecast.com ('Good surf at all stages of the tide') and WannaSurf ('All tides') both say all tides, recorded as contradicting. The Inertia says low tide throws hardest but makes the paddle-out harder (no preference). Size: WannaSurf gives under 3 ft to 12 ft+ and its description says it holds 15 ft+, matching the profile's 3-15 ft. Period: still no source with numbers (surf-forecast only says clean groundswells prevail). Bathymetry is backed by USGS and JCR abstracts (ebb-tidal delta focuses wave energy on the central/southern beach) plus dated 2022 magazine evidence that the bars shift constantly. The surf-forecast page has template glitches: its 'Reviews' block describes 'Porthcawl Point' and it lists Kellys Cove (the north end of Ocean Beach) as a separate break 5 km away. Classification note: the USGS 70158958 entry is a conference paper catalogued by USGS. It is kept as official (government geological survey), as in the earlier pass. The JCR abstract is peer_reviewed. The Stormrider break page for Ocean Beach (/break/ocean-beach) renders its text only with JavaScript, so nothing could be cited from it.

## Ideal conditions

Directions are compass degrees the swell or wind comes FROM, ranges clockwise. Heights keep the scale each source states (breaking face, Hawaiian, swell or relative to the surfer); the app's sizes are breaking face heights in feet. Sources are numbered as in [Sources](#sources).

### Swell height

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Minimum suitable | 3 ft | documented | S3 | `wave_height_min_ft` 3 ft (breaking face) |
| Ideal range | — | not documented | — | no separate setting; working range 3–15 ft |
| Maximum suitable | 15 ft+ (no upper limit stated) | documented | S3, S7, S8 | `wave_height_max_ft` 15 ft (breaking face) |

Notes:

- **Minimum suitable**: WannaSurf says it starts working at less than 1 m / 3 ft; the template does not say whether this is face or offshore swell height.
  - S3 (WannaSurf): “Starts working at Less than 1m / 3ft and holds up to 4m+ / 12ft...The place holds 15'+”
- **Ideal range**: No excerpt gives an ideal size.
- **Maximum suitable**: WannaSurf's template says it holds 4 m+ / 12 ft and its description says 15 ft+ (scale not stated), Unofficial Networks says it can handle just about as big as it gets depending on the sandbars and swell direction, and Stormrider says it needs big guns.
  - S3 (WannaSurf): “Starts working at Less than 1m / 3ft and holds up to 4m+ / 12ft...The place holds 15'+”
  - S7 (Unofficial Networks): “it can handle just about as big as it gets, depending on the current shape of the sandbars and specific direction of the swell”
  - S8 (Stormrider Surf Guides): “A full quiver should include big guns for out of control Ocean Beach and Mavericks”

### Swell direction

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ideal bearing | best range: 225–315° (SW to NW, clockwise); ideal: 270° (W) | documented | S2, S6, S7 | `optimal_swell_direction` 255–295° (WSW to WNW, clockwise) |
| Acceptable range | — | not documented | — | `swell_window` 190–320° (S to NW, clockwise) |

Notes:

- **Ideal bearing**: Surf-Forecast gives west as the ideal swell direction and Unofficial Networks says NW, W and SW swells do best; The Inertia says 'north swells' bring the most size and best waves, a colloquial term with no compass direction.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “Clean groundswells prevail and the ideal swell direction is from the west.”
  - S7 (Unofficial Networks): “NW, W, and SW swells do the best at lighting up OB”
  - S6 (The Inertia): “some south swells in the middle of the summer will pass by OB completely...But if we're talking north swells, Ocean Beach is where you'll consistently find the most size and the best waves”
- **Acceptable range**: No excerpt gives an outer swell window.
- **Blocked directions**: The Inertia says some south swells in the middle of summer pass by Ocean Beach completely; no degrees are given.
  - S6 (The Inertia): “some south swells in the middle of the summer will pass by OB completely...But if we're talking north swells, Ocean Beach is where you'll consistently find the most size and the best waves”
- **Exposure**: Surf-Forecast calls it an exposed beach break.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “an exposed beach break that is usually a safe bet...The beach breaks offer lefts and rights.”

### Seasonality

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Prime months | Dec, Jan, Feb | documented | S1, S2, S7, S10 | `best_months` Sep, Oct, Nov, Dec, Jan, Feb |
| Secondary season | fall; early spring | documented | S7, S10 | no setting |
| Swell sources | north swells (winter) | documented | S1, S6 | no setting |
| Wind patterns | — | not documented | — | no setting |

Notes:

- **Prime months**: Surf-Forecast favours winter, Wikipedia says it can be world class in large winter swells, Unofficial Networks says winter or perhaps fall, and SurferToday (search summary) fall, winter and early spring; winter is common to all, read as December-February.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “Winter is the favoured time of year for surfing here.”
  - S1 (Wikipedia): “when breaking well — can be world class, especially during large swells in the winter months”
  - S7 (Unofficial Networks): “you'll probably have to be down here sometime in the winter, or perhaps in the fall”
  - S10 (SurferToday): “the best period of the year to surf Ocean Beach is during fall, winter, and early spring”
- **Secondary season**: Unofficial Networks adds 'perhaps in the fall' and SurferToday (search summary, not read directly) names fall and early spring alongside winter.
  - S7 (Unofficial Networks): “you'll probably have to be down here sometime in the winter, or perhaps in the fall”
  - S10 (SurferToday): “the best period of the year to surf Ocean Beach is during fall, winter, and early spring”
- **Swell sources**: The Inertia says north swells bring the most size and best waves (no compass direction) and Wikipedia credits large winter swells; no excerpt names the generating storms.
  - S6 (The Inertia): “some south swells in the middle of the summer will pass by OB completely...But if we're talking north swells, Ocean Beach is where you'll consistently find the most size and the best waves”
  - S1 (Wikipedia): “when breaking well — can be world class, especially during large swells in the winter months”
- **Wind patterns**: No excerpt describes seasonal or prevailing winds.

### Geography

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Break type | beach | documented | S2, S3, S11 | `break_type` beach, `wave_direction` both |
| Orientation | — | not documented | — | nearshore-model shore normal estimated as the centre of the optimal swell direction (275° (W)) |
| Exposure | exposed | documented | S2 | no setting |
| Bathymetry | sandy, constantly shifting sandbars in two rows; the ebb-tidal delta off the Golden Gate shields parts of the coast and focuses wave energy on the central and southern beach, and has contracted | documented | S3, S4, S5, S6, S9, S10, S11, S16 | measured BlueTopo values in physical_profiles.json |

Notes:

- **Break type**: Surf-Forecast and WannaSurf call it a beach break with lefts and rights, and SURFER (search summary) one of the heaviest, most dynamic beach breaks in the world.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “an exposed beach break that is usually a safe bet...The beach breaks offer lefts and rights.”
  - S3 (WannaSurf): “TypeBeach-break DirectionRight and left BottomSandy PowerHollow, Powerful, Fun”
  - S11 (SURFER Magazine): “one of the heaviest, most dynamic beachbreaks in the world. The sandbars shift often, so the lineup can change within a single session.”
- **Orientation**: No excerpt gives the beach orientation (the BlueTopo contour fit in the evidence claim text is the app's own processing, not an excerpt).
- **Exposure**: Surf-Forecast calls it an exposed beach break.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “an exposed beach break that is usually a safe bet...The beach breaks offer lefts and rights.”
- **Bathymetry**: WannaSurf gives a sandy bottom, The Inertia says the sandbars are always changing, SURFER and SurferToday (search summaries) describe two rows of sandbars that hold large winter waves, USGS (2011) and JCR (2012) say the ebb-tidal delta focuses wave energy and has contracted, ScienceDirect (search summary) quantifies the 1956-2005 loss, and NOAA BlueTopo tiles cover the break.
  - S3 (WannaSurf): “BottomSandy”
  - S6 (The Inertia): “Thanks to the current, the sandbars are always changing too.”
  - S11 (SURFER Magazine): “3 miles of shifty, hulking peaks blitzing two distinct rows of sandbars. Waves are smaller on the inner bar, and bigger swells break further out.”
  - S4 (U.S. Geological Survey): “The prominent bathymetry of the ebb tidal delta protects some of the coast from extreme storm waves, but the delta also focuses wave energy toward the central and southern portions of Ocean Beach.”
  - S5 (Journal of Coastal Research (BioOne)): “alongshore variability in forcing introduced by varying nearshore bathymetry...ebb-tidal delta, which in turn reduced the regional grain size and modified wave focusing patterns along Ocean Beach”
  - S9 (ScienceDirect (Elsevier)): “compared 1956 and 2005 bathymetry. It found the 150 km² ebb-tidal delta lost about 76 million m³ of sediment and contracted by roughly 1 km”
  - S10 (SurferToday): “these sandbanks can also hold large waves during winter, making it a testing site for experienced and hardcore surfers.”
  - S16 (NOAA Office of Coast Survey): “This dataset is a multi-layered raster and part of NOAA Office of Coast Survey BlueTopo bathymetry...The vertical coordinate reference system for this product is NAVD88”
